summary: Provides up-to-date recommendations for the secure use of TLS and DTLS, which protect data for many application protocols. It responds to attacks seen over the years on common cipher suites and modes of operation. It obsoletes RFC 7525. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Locks get picked, so lock advice changes. This is the current list of which settings are safe for secure connections, and which old ones to stop using.

subtitle: The current checklist for configuring TLS and DTLS so they actually protect your traffic.

tldr.problem: Years of attacks on TLS and DTLS, including on the most common cipher suites and modes, left implementers and operators needing current guidance on how to use them securely.
tldr.mechanism: This Best Current Practice sets MUST, SHOULD and MUST NOT rules for protocol versions, strict TLS, session resumption, renegotiation, SNI, ALPN, cipher suites, key sizes and key usage limits.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7525 and pushes deployments from TLS 1.2 toward TLS 1.3, while keeping TLS 1.2 mandatory to support.

today: RFC 9325 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 195) that obsoletes RFC 7525 and has been updated by RFC 9852 and RFC 10015. It updates RFC 5288 and RFC 6066.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 9325 gives recommendations for deployed services and software that use TLS and DTLS to protect protocols such as HTTP, IMAP, POP, SIP, SMTP and XMPP. Transport protocols that reuse the TLS handshake, such as QUIC, are not directly in scope. Unless a rule is marked as applying to only one of them, it applies to both TLS and DTLS.

It replaces RFC 7525, which was written while the industry was moving to TLS 1.2. That move is now largely complete and TLS 1.3 is widely available, so the guidance is updated and the stated goal is to encourage migration of most uses of TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3. It also updates RFC 5288 (because of an attack on AES-GCM nonce reuse) and RFC 6066 (because of the ALPACA attack).

The recommendations are minimums for the vast majority of deployments, a floor and not a ceiling. The RFC warns that a BCP about security is a point-in-time statement, and says it is too early to make recommendations on post-quantum cryptography.
sections.eli5: This is the safety rulebook for secure connections, updated because the old one aged and bad guys found new tricks.

sections.title: Protocol Versions
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT negotiate SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. The change for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 from SHOULD NOT in RFC 7525 to MUST NOT matches RFC 8996. Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2, because it is deployed more widely than TLS 1.3 and, if the recommendations are followed, is as safe. Implementations SHOULD support TLS 1.3 and, if they do, MUST prefer it over earlier versions.

New transport protocols that integrate the TLS or DTLS handshake or record layer MUST use only TLS or DTLS 1.3. New application protocols that use TLS for channel encryption MUST integrate with both 1.2 and 1.3, although in rare cases where broad interoperability is not a concern designers MAY skip 1.2.

For DTLS, implementations MUST NOT negotiate DTLS 1.0, MUST support DTLS 1.2, and SHOULD support DTLS 1.3 and prefer it. TLS 1.2 clients MUST NOT fall back to earlier versions, so the downgrade SCSV mechanism is no longer needed for clients. The BCP does not extend to any future TLS version.
sections.eli5: Old locks that are known to be broken must never be used. Use the newest lock if both sides have it, and keep the middle-aged one around so more doors still work.

sections.title: Strict TLS, Compression, Resumption and Renegotiation
sections.content:
Strict TLS. To resist SSL stripping and STARTTLS command injection, when a protocol has both a TLS-only port and a dynamic upgrade, the TLS-only method MUST be supported and administrators MUST configure it in preference. When only upgrade exists, implementations MUST offer a strict policy forbidding plaintext and administrators MUST use it. Web clients and servers must support HSTS, and servers SHOULD use it.

Compression. TLS 1.2 implementations SHOULD NOT support TLS-level compression because of attacks such as CRIME. TLS 1.3 removed it. Compression at higher layers (BREACH) can only be mitigated outside TLS.

Session resumption. Resumption information MUST be authenticated and encrypted with a strong cipher. Ticket-encryption keys MUST be changed regularly (for example once every week) and old keys destroyed. Ticket validity MUST be limited, for example to half the key validity. A TLS 1.2 server SHOULD NOT resume sessions older than two key rotation periods. For TLS 1.3, servers SHOULD select the psk_dhe_ke mode and answer with a key_share to keep forward secrecy.

Renegotiation (TLS 1.2 only). Clients and servers MUST implement renegotiation_info, clients MUST send it, and a client MUST fail the handshake if the server does not acknowledge it. TLS 1.2 implementations MUST support extended_master_secret against the Triple Handshake attack. Multiplexed protocols SHOULD follow RFC 9113 advice on post-handshake authentication.
sections.eli5: Always use the secure door, never start talking in the open and hope to lock up later. Change the spare keys often, and ignore requests to redo the handshake the old, risky way.

sections.title: SNI, ALPN, Multi-Server Setups and 0-RTT
sections.content:
TLS implementations MUST support Server Name Indication (SNI) for protocols that benefit from it, though using it is a local policy decision. SNI leaks the target domain, and Encrypted Client Hello was still being worked on at the time. To prevent ALPACA attacks, a server that does not recognize the presented name SHOULD fail with a fatal unrecognized_name(112) alert, which updates RFC 6066. Clients SHOULD abort if the certificate has a different host name than the one they sent.

Implementations MUST support ALPN. Servers are advised to send a fatal no_application_protocol alert if they support none of the client's protocols, and clients SHOULD abort if the server acknowledges ALPN but selects no protocol from the list. Protocol developers are strongly encouraged to register an ALPN identifier.

When several services share a domain, or several servers provide the same service, they SHOULD provide equivalent security levels, so an attacker cannot steer a client to the weakest one (cross-protocol and DROWN-style attacks). For TLS 1.3 0-RTT data, applications MUST avoid it unless an explicit specification clarifies when it is appropriate and secure.
sections.eli5: If a visitor asks for a room that does not exist, say so instead of guessing. And do not let a fast-pass shortcut skip important safety checks.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT negotiate NULL-encryption suites, RC4 suites, or suites offering less than 112 bits of security (including export-level encryption). They SHOULD NOT negotiate suites with less than 128 bits, static RSA key transport (TLS_RSA_WITH_*), or non-ephemeral DH and ECDH. They MUST support and prefer forward-secret suites, but TLS 1.2 implementations SHOULD NOT negotiate finite-field ephemeral DH (TLS_DHE_*).

For TLS 1.2, four AEAD suites are RECOMMENDED: ECDHE with RSA or ECDSA, each with AES-128-GCM-SHA256 or AES-256-GCM-SHA384. Clients SHOULD offer TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 first, and servers MUST prefer it over weaker suites. CBC suites SHOULD NOT be used unless encrypt_then_mac is negotiated. Clients and servers SHOULD support P-256 and X25519. For TLS 1.3 the RFC defers to RFC 8446 for cipher suites.

Key sizes: DH keys of at least 2048 bits are REQUIRED for DHE, curves under 224 bits MUST NOT be used, and RSA server certificates MUST have at least a 2048-bit modulus. SHA-256 is RECOMMENDED and SHA-1 and MD5 MUST NOT be used. The Truncated HMAC extension MUST NOT be used. Limits on key usage: senders approaching the confidentiality limit SHOULD rotate the key, and for AES-GCM the RFC recommends a limit of 2^24.5 records.
sections.eli5: Use strong, modern locks, and change the lock on a door that has been opened too many times. Throw away locks that anyone can pick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Host name validation is security-critical. Without it, TLS shows only that the certificate is valid and the peer has the private key, not that the connection ends at the intended endpoint. A host name found by an insecure cleartext DNS query SHOULD NOT be used as a reference identifier.

AES-GCM nonce reuse has been found in deployed TLS 1.2 stacks, so it is RECOMMENDED that TLS 1.2 implementations fill nonce_explicit with the 64-bit sequence number, strengthening RFC 5288.

Forward secrecy protects recorded conversations if long-term keys are later stolen, and the document advocates strict use of forward-secret ciphers. DH exponent reuse can undo it, so implementations SHOULD NOT use static finite-field DH or reuse ephemeral ones, and servers reusing ECDH keys SHOULD use a safe curve such as X25519 or check received points.

Certificate revocation has no complete solution. Implementations MUST implement a strategy to distrust revoked certificates, and servers SHOULD support OCSP and OCSP stapling. The Multiple Certificate Status extension is no longer recommended.
sections.eli5: Check that you reached the right house, not just that the door has a lock. And use a new secret every visit, so one stolen key cannot open old diaries.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7525
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the normative changes. Highlights: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 go from SHOULD NOT to MUST NOT; TLS 1.3 is added at SHOULD level, with similar changes for DTLS; guidance is added for new protocols, multiplexed protocols, ALPN and SNI, and key usage limits; and new attacks are covered (ALPACA, Raccoon, Logjam, and nonce-disrespecting adversaries).

For TLS 1.2, finite-field DH is now SHOULD NOT, 2048-bit DH is a MUST, the minimum ECDH curve size is 224 bits (earlier 192), extended_master_secret is a MUST, ticket validity limits are MUST, and X25519 is recommended beside P-256. For TLS 1.3 it adds 0-RTT guidance and a SHOULD for forward secrecy on resumption.
sections.eli5: The new rulebook is stricter about old locks and adds rules for the newest lock.
